summary:
Kelantan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

All 13 states of Malaysia and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Kelantan's own layer was rewritten after litigation narrowed it. In February 2024 the Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 on federalism grounds, leaving the federal Penal Code offences fully intact. In August 2026 the Kelantan state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026, replacing those 16 struck-down provisions. The Bill legislates covering of aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts. Clause 15 mandates that Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law, and the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

The new decency provisions are backed by whipping of three to six strokes, fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years. The enactment is in force and is being applied by the Syariah courts. A case in February 2026 was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing and gender-change offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, with detainees' faces and personal details leaked to pre-tipped media and 31 foreign nationals held among them before their embassies intervened.
tangentialFactors:
Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and the 16 Kelantan provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds. The sequence of invalidation by the national courts followed by prompt re-enactment by the Kelantan assembly in August 2026 documents institutional determination to keep gender nonconformity criminalised under Islamic criminal law.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law anywhere in Malaysia.
localsOnly:
The Sharia cross-dressing and gender-change offences reach Muslims only, so Kelantan residents who are Muslim fall under provisions that do not touch non-Muslim visitors. Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the scope of the offence to enforcement discretion.

Kelantan's Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026, passed on 13 August 2026, is in force and being applied by the Syariah courts. It replaces the 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down, and it legislates covering of aurat, gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, with whipping of three to six strokes, fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years. A February 2026 proceeding was the first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change.

Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed cross-dressing enactments, three of them also barring women from posing as men. Federal Penal Code sections 377A and 377B apply to residents regardless of consent and are not limited to Malaysians.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity, no recognition of same-sex partnerships, and no access to state-supported channels other than the mukhayyam retreats, which are framed as rehabilitation. Litigation to date has produced relief on federalism grounds rather than on constitutional rights grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state how "gender change" is defined in clause 15 or elsewhere in the 2026 Bill, whether medical transition, legal marker change, or outward presentation is captured, or whether the offence requires an act, an intent, or a diagnosis. That scope is unresolved on the available sources.

Whether whipping under the new decency provisions has been ordered or carried out since enforcement began in 2026 is not sourced here. The inventory confirms the penalties and that the enactment is being applied, but records no sentence.

The February 2026 Kelantan Syariah Court proceeding is identified as the first state case involving gender change, but its facts, the person charged, and the outcome are not sourced in the inventory.

Whether the 2026 Bill's provisions have been applied to any non-Muslim, or whether the state layer remains confined to Muslims as the parent framework states, is not addressed by these sources and should be treated as unresolved.

Enforcement frequency in Kelantan after August 2026, and whether raid-based operations of the kind documented in Kuala Lumpur in November 2025 have occurred in Kelantan, are not covered by the inventory.
